name: Nora Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Nora, thanks for your time. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and what you really think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the Lund farm, which is free-range hens, potatoes and about sixty beef cattle. I start at six collecting eggs from three thousand hens, then it's the grading room, where a machine sorts by size and I check for cracks. Afternoons it's whatever Erik Lund needs, feeding the cattle or picking stones off the potato field. I've been there two years and I still get the egg counts wrong sometimes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the routine, honestly. Same hens, same shed, same jobs, and I know where I am. What's hard is the pay, and my boyfriend Luca's hours at the parcel firm keep changing. We rent a flat above the bakery in the village, and we've got about two months of money saved.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools for anything?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. I don't see the point. Luca's firm uses something to plan his routes, and he moans about it every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because most of it sounded like nonsense anyway. I wouldn't post anything, I never do. At work I'd tell Erik he can stop reading those farming magazines about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't fix much for us. Egg prices from the supermarket are already squeezing Erik, and he's talked about cutting the flock by a thousand birds. Luca's firm cut two routes last spring, and he lost Saturday shifts. Nothing changes means those worries carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the job right, especially the egg counts. We'd cut the takeaways and Luca's football subscription to save a bit more. I'd ask Erik straight whether my hours are safe if he cuts the flock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like normal life, which isn't exactly relaxing. I'm a bit tense, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would cutting the flock by a thousand birds mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A thousand fewer hens on the Lund farm means maybe an hour less work a day for me in the grading room. Erik is fair, but he's not a charity. I'd probably go down to four days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Luca manage on four days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd manage, but only just. The rent above the bakery is the big one, and we'd stop putting anything aside. It would mean no holiday again this year.

I'd tell Erik to stop reading **robot magazines**.
I wouldn't **post** anything, because I never do.
think: **Egg prices** already squeeze Erik, and he may cut **birds**.
Luca lost **Saturday shifts** when his parcel firm cut routes.
Nothing changing means those **worries carry on**.
do: Keep my head down and get the **egg counts** right.
Ask Erik whether my **hours are safe** if he cuts the flock.
feel: **Tense**, the same as now, because normal life isn't relaxing.
S0.quote: A thousand fewer hens on the Lund farm means maybe an hour less work a day for me in the grading room.
fieldNote: Her worries come from **egg prices** and Luca's **shift cuts**, not AI.
She'd quietly drop to **four days** rather than look elsewhere.
She trusts **routine** and is direct with her boss about hours.

steps.text: Keep collecting and grading eggs for Erik Lund as now
Cancel takeaways and Luca's football subscription

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what always happens: whoever does it cheaper wins, and the rest of us adjust. I wouldn't blame anyone in particular. I'd say it to Luca and my mum, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's Luca I'd worry about first. His route planning is already software, and now the AI does the booking and the customer messages too, so the firm needs fewer people in the depot. My job is hands-on, but Erik has been looking at an egg-collecting robot for the sheds. If that comes, my mornings are gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe a hundred a month instead of fifty, by cutting the car to one tank a fortnight. I'd wait and see what Erik decides about the robot before I panic. I'm not going to learn computers just because people say I should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a slow squeeze. Not a disaster, but a squeeze on both of us at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. What would make you stop waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Erik orders the egg robot, I'd start looking that week. There are other farms nearby, the dairy and the big potato grower. I'd rather move to a farm that still needs hands than learn to babysit a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Luca if his depot cut more people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Luca not to wait for them to pick him, and to ask the bakery downstairs about early shifts. He'd hate it. But the bakery needs a driver at five in the morning, and that's a person, for now.

say: Whoever does it **cheaper wins**, and the rest of us **adjust**.
I wouldn't **blame** anyone, and I'd say it to family, not **online**.
think: **Luca's depot** feels it first, with fewer people needed.

If the robot comes, my **mornings are gone**.
do: Save **a hundred a month** by cutting the car to one tank a fortnight.
**Wait** to see what Erik decides about the robot.
Look at other farms the **same week** if the robot is ordered.
feel: A **slow squeeze** on both of us at once.
S1.quote: I'd rather move to a farm that still needs hands than learn to babysit a machine.
fieldNote: Her first worry is **Luca's job**, where desk tasks are already going to software.
She'd **refuse** to retrain into tech and look for another hands-on farm instead.
Her stance is **non-ideological**: cheaper wins, nobody to blame.

steps.text: Save a hundred a month instead of fifty

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody voted for this and nobody's ready, and the government had better sort something quickly. I still wouldn't post anything. With the girls from the village I'd probably just say we're all in it together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, it scares me. In 2028 the AI takes Luca's depot jobs, the bookings, the customer calls, maybe the route planners. Then around 2031 the robots arrive, and a robot can collect eggs, sort them and pick stones all night. In 2028 the AI takes Luca's depot jobs, then robots take my egg collecting, and that's both of us gone within three years. I don't have a plan for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, we'd give up the flat above the bakery and move into my mum's spare room to save the rent, maybe six hundred a month. All our spare money goes into savings. If either of us loses work, I'd go straight to the job centre and claim whatever there is. I'd keep working at Lund's until the last day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like falling. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving into your mum's spare room at twenty-seven. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Horrible, honestly. Mum would be nice about it, but it's a step back. Luca would sleep on the sofa the first week out of pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep working at Lund's until the last day. Why stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Erik's been good to me, and a wage is a wage. Every month at Lund's is a month of rent saved. I'm not going to jump before I'm pushed.

say: The government had better **sort something** quickly.
With the village girls I'd say we're all **in it together**.
think: In **2028** AI takes Luca's depot jobs.
Around **2031** robots can collect eggs and pick stones all night.
That's **both of us gone** within three years, with no plan.
do: Move into **Mum's spare room** to save about six hundred a month.
Claim **job centre** help straight away if either of us loses work.
S2.quote: In 2028 the AI takes Luca's depot jobs, then robots take my egg collecting, and that's both of us gone within three years.
fieldNote: She sees the **double hit**: Luca's desk-linked job in 2028, her hands-on job around 2031.
Moving to **Mum's** is a painful step back, but she'd do it fast.
Loyalty to **Erik** keeps her working to the end rather than jumping first.

steps.text: Move into Mum's spare room to save six hundred a month
Put all spare money from both wages into savings
Claim job centre support if Luca or I lose work
Keep working at the Lund farm until the last day

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years sounds like a lot until you're in it. I'd tell people to save, not spend. I'd still keep it to the kitchen table, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's the same ending, just later. The AI comes in 2031 and takes the office side of things, and Luca's depot. Robots arrive around 2034, and that's my eggs and potatoes. I'd be thirty-five with no trade except collecting eggs, and I'm not quick with new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stay in the flat for now but save harder, a hundred and fifty a month. In the third or fourth year, before the robots, I'd do the care assistant course my mum did, because old people need hands for a long time. I'd wait a year or two to see how fast things move before I start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels heavy. Like a date on the calendar I don't want to look at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why care work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my mum's been a care assistant for twenty years and she's never once been short of work. It's hands-on, like the hens, but with people. I don't love the idea, but it's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a year or two. Is waiting a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. Luca says I always leave things too late, and he's usually right. But I'm not starting a course for a world that hasn't arrived yet.

say: **Five years** sounds like a lot until you're in it.
I'd keep that talk to the **kitchen table**, not online.
think: Robots reach my eggs and potatoes around **2034**.
At thirty-five I'd have **no trade** and I'm slow with new things.
do: Save **150** a month while staying in the flat.
Start the **care assistant course** in year three or four.
**Wait** a year or **two** before starting anything.
S3.quote: My mum's been a care assistant for twenty years and she's never once been short of work.
fieldNote: Extra time **delays** her fear but doesn't change it; she still expects both incomes to go.
She'd follow her **mum's path** into care, the only route she trusts.
She admits **waiting** is risky but won't act before she sees it.

steps.text: Save a hundred and fifty a month while renting the flat
Take the care assistant course before robots reach the Lund farm
Wait a year or two to see the pace first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and anything could happen in ten years. I'd tell people not to panic. That's what I'd say to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it gives me breathing room, but I know myself. The AI comes in 2036, robots around 2039, and I'd be nearly forty. I'd probably keep working at Lund's for most of that, and Luca and I might have kids by then, which makes it scarier, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Lund's for now and keep saving what we can, about a hundred a month. I'd see how things look in five years before changing anything. Maybe then the care course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels far away, which is nice. But it's still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Would this change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not now, no. We'd still want kids in a few years. But I'd want the care course done before they're at school, so I'm not starting over with toddlers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So which is it: no plan for five years, or the care course before the kids are at school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point, those don't fit. I suppose I'd do the course around year five, when it's still early enough. I'm better at plans when they have a date on them.

say: **Ten years** is a long time; **anything** could happen.
That's what I'd tell **anyone who asked**, at work or in the village.
think: It gives me **breathing room**, but I know myself.
I'd be nearly **forty** when robots arrive around 2039.
Having **kids** by then makes it scarier.
do: Carry on at **Lund's** and save about **a hundred** a month.
Check how things look in **five years** before changing anything.
Do the **care course** around year five, before kids start school.
feel: **Far away**, which is nice, but it's **still there**.
S4.quote: I'm better at plans when they have a date on them.
fieldNote: Even with ten years she expects to **lose the farm job** before forty.

Save about a hundred a month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Luca and I would both be out of work within three years and we'd have nothing to fall back on but my mum. What would help is proper money while you retrain, so you don't have to choose between rent and a course. And honest notice from employers, a year at least.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about couples. Everyone asks about one person's job, but rent's paid by two. If both jobs go in the same few years, it doesn't matter which one went first.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks about one person's job, but rent's paid by two.
portrait: Nora is a **27-year-old** junior worker on the Lund farm, collecting eggs and grading them.
She likes **routine**, never uses AI, and keeps her views to the kitchen table.
She rents with **Luca**, a parcel driver, so she always thinks about **two jobs**.
Faster AGI pictures make her **alarmed**, because both incomes could go within years.
Her fallback is **care work**, like her mum, but she tends to wait.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Luca would both lose work within three **years**.
whatWouldHelp: **Money while retraining**, so rent and a course don't compete.
At least **a year's notice** from employers.
